claim: After an initial stage of local analysis within the retina and early visual pathways, the human visual system creates a structured representation of the visual scene by co-selecting image elements that are part of behaviorally relevant objects.
source: After an initial stage of local analysis within the retina and early visual pathways, the human visual system creates a structured representation of the visual scene by co-selecting image elements that are part of behaviorally relevant objects.
evidence: This is a general statement about visual processing that draws from established understanding of visual system organization.

claim: The mechanisms underlying perceptual organization process are only partially understood.
source: The mechanisms underlying this perceptual organization process are only partially understood.
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Perceptual grouping of two-dimensional image-regions is associated with the gradual spread of object-based attention.
source: We here investigate the time-course of perceptual grouping of two-dimensional image-regions by measuring the reaction times of human participants and report that it is associated with the gradual spread of object-based attention.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript measuring reaction times.

claim: Attention spreads fastest over large and homogeneous areas.
source: Attention spreads fastest over large and homogeneous areas and is slowed down at locations that require small-scale processing.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental results showing RT patterns in Experiments 1 and 2.

claim: Attention is slowed down at locations that require small-scale processing.
source: Attention spreads fastest over large and homogeneous areas and is slowed down at locations that require small-scale processing.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing longer RTs near edges and in narrow regions.

claim: The time-course of the object-based selection process is well explained by a 'growth-cone' model.
source: We find that the time-course of the object-based selection process is well explained by a 'growth-cone' model, which selects surface elements in an incremental, scale-dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by regression analyses showing the growth-cone model explains more variance than alternative models.

claim: The growth-cone model selects surface elements in an incremental, scale-dependent manner.
source: We find that the time-course of the object-based selection process is well explained by a 'growth-cone' model, which selects surface elements in an incremental, scale-dependent manner.
evidence: This describes the theoretical mechanism of the growth-cone model.

claim: The visual cortical hierarchy can implement scale-dependent spread of object-based attention by leveraging different receptive field sizes in distinct cortical areas.
source: We discuss how the visual cortical hierarchy can implement this scale-dependent spread of object-based attention, leveraging the different receptive field sizes in distinct cortical areas.
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal based on known properties of visual cortex and the experimental findings.

claim: Neurophysiological studies over the past 40 years have revealed that the neuronal representation of an object in low-level areas of the visual cortex consists of a set of simple features such as colors and edge orientations.
source: Neurophysiological studies over the past 40 years have revealed that the neuronal representation of an object in low-level areas of the visual cortex consists of a set of simple features such as colors and edge orientations.
evidence: This refers to established findings from decades of neurophysiological research.

claim: Our perception is structured because our visual system groups features into objects.
source: Our perception is much more structured, because our visual system groups the features into objects.
evidence: This is based on established understanding of visual perception.

claim: The grouping process appears to be effortless because we hardly ever perceive features in isolation.
source: Introspectively, this grouping process appears to be effortless because we hardly ever perceive features in isolation.
evidence: This is based on introspective observation and general knowledge about perception.

claim: Palmer and Rock (1994) suggested that perceptual grouping occurs instantaneously and in parallel if features are connected to each other.
source: One influential theory suggested that perceptual grouping occurs instantaneously and in parallel if features are connected to each other, i.e. 'uniformly connected' (Palmer and Rock, 1994).
evidence: This cites a specific theory from prior literature.

claim: Object recognition can be extremely fast and pre-attentive.
source: Such a rapid grouping process would be in line with studies demonstrating that object recognition can be extremely fast and pre-attentive (Thorpe et al., 1996; Moore and Egeth, 1997; Treisman, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: High-speed object recognition presumably relies on feedforward processing, leveraging the hierarchy of features represented in the visual cortex.
source: High-speed object recognition presumably relies on feedforward processing, leveraging the hierarchy of features represented in the visual cortex.
evidence: This is an inference based on computational models and neurophysiological understanding.

claim: Neurons in lower areas coding for elementary features rapidly propagate activity to shape selective neurons in higher visual areas.
source: Neurons in lower areas coding for elementary features rapidly propagate activity to shape selective neurons in higher visual areas (Hung et al., 2005; DiCarlo et al., 2012), grouping features into more complex constellations (Roelfsema, 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citations to neurophysiological studies.

claim: Perceptual grouping can coincide with object recognition.
source: grouping features into more complex constellations (Roelfsema, 2006) so that perceptual grouping coincides with object recognition (Biederman et al., 1987; Nakayama et al., 1989; Driver and Baylis, 1996; Pelli et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: There exist conditions where perceptual grouping requires a slow and serial process.
source: However, there also exist conditions where perceptual grouping requires a slow and serial process (Roelfsema, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Curve tracing is an example of a task that invokes a serial, incremental grouping operation.
source: Curve tracing is an example of a task that invokes such a serial, incremental grouping operation (Jolicoeur et al., 1986; Jolicoeur and Ingleton, 1991; Pringle and Egeth, 1988; Roelfsema and Houtkamp, 2011) when participants group contour elements of an elongated curve.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies on curve tracing.

claim: In curve tracing tasks, reaction times increase linearly with the length of the curve.
source: In this task, reaction times increase linearly with the length of the curve.
evidence: This is a well-established finding from curve tracing studies, as shown in Figure 1a.

claim: In curve tracing, attention gradually spreads over the curve until it reaches the target.
source: Subjects first direct their attention to the red fixation point and attention then gradually spreads over the curve until it reaches the green circle (Scholte et al., 2001; Houtkamp et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Curve-tracing is implemented in the visual cortex as the propagation of enhanced neuronal activity over the curve's representation.
source: This process is implemented in the visual cortex as the propagation of enhanced neuronal activity over the curve's representation (Pooresmaeili and Roelfsema, 2014) (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to neurophysiological work and illustrated in Figure 1b.

claim: Curve-tracing is size invariant.
source: Curve-tracing is size invariant (Jolicoeur and Ingleton, 1991) so that the reaction time of observers depends little on the viewing distance.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Size invariance in curve tracing can be explained if perceptual grouping occurs at multiple levels of the visual cortical hierarchy.
source: Size invariance can be explained if perceptual grouping occurs at multiple levels of the visual cortical hierarchy (Roelfsema and Houtkamp, 2011; Pooresmaeili and Roelfsema, 2014).
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation supported by citations.

claim: When curves are nearby, perceptual grouping requires the high spatial resolution provided by low-level areas where neurons have small receptive fields.
source: When curves are nearby, perceptual grouping requires the high spatial resolution provided by low-level areas where neurons have small receptive fields (RFs) and horizontal connections interconnect neurons with RFs that are nearby in visual space so that progress is slow.
evidence: This is an inference based on known properties of visual cortex organization.

claim: If curves are farther apart, neurons in higher areas with larger receptive fields can speed up the grouping process.
source: If curves are farther apart, however, neurons in higher areas can take over and their larger RFs could speed up the grouping process (Pooresmaeili and Roelfsema, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and is an inference about neural mechanisms.

claim: Size invariance occurs when subjects solve a maze, because paths are followed at a higher speed if the distance between the walls is larger.
source: Size invariance also occurs when subjects solve a maze, because paths are followed at a higher speed if the distance between the walls is larger (Crowe et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The uniform connectedness hypothesis predicts that image regions with homogenous surface properties are grouped instantaneously.
source: The uniform connectedness hypothesis by Palmer and Rock, 1994 will serve as baseline. These authors suggested that image regions with homogenous surface properties are grouped instantaneously (Palmer and Rock, 1994) so that the reaction time should not depend on the placement of cues within a white region enclosed by a black contour (as in Figure 2a).
evidence: This describes a theoretical prediction from prior literature.

claim: The pixel-by-pixel model predicts that grouping is realized by spreading attention across pixels of the same color at a fixed speed.
source: The second model has been called 'pixel-by-pixel' in the context of curve-tracing (McCormick and Jolicoeur, 1994; Jolicoeur and Ingleton, 1991). Grouping is realized by spreading attention across pixels of the same color, at a fixed speed (Figure 2b).
evidence: This describes a theoretical model with citations to prior work.

claim: In the pixel-by-pixel model, processing time is proportional to the length of the shortest path through the object.
source: Spreading starts at one of the cues and processing time is proportional to the length of the shortest path through the object.
evidence: This describes a prediction of the pixel-by-pixel model.

claim: The growth-cone model predicts that grouping speed depends on the size of homogeneous image regions.
source: The third model is the growth-cone model (Figure 2c), inspired by models for curve tracing (Pooresmaeili and Roelfsema, 2014; McCormick and Jolicoeur, 1994; Jolicoeur et al., 1986) and visual routines (Ullman, 1984; Roelfsema et al., 2000). The growth-cone model predicts that grouping speed depends on the size of homogeneous image regions.
evidence: This describes the growth-cone model with citations to related prior work.

claim: In the growth-cone model, spreading is fast within large regions and slows down in narrow regions.
source: Spreading is fast within large regions and slows down in narrow regions.
evidence: This describes a key prediction of the growth-cone model.

claim: The growth-cone model is scale invariant because the total spreading time does not depend on variations in the overall size of the picture.
source: This model is scale invariant because the total spreading time does not depend on variations in the overall size of the picture, caused e.g. by changes in viewing distance.
evidence: This describes a property of the growth-cone model.

claim: The filling-in model predicts that the grouping signal spreads inwards from the boundaries of the cued object.
source: The fourth model is one where the grouping signal spreads inwards from the boundaries of the cued object so that the response time increases with the distance between the cue and the boundary (Figure 2d) (Komatsu, 2006).
evidence: This describes the filling-in model with a citation.

claim: A filling-in process has been proposed for brightness perception.
source: Such a 'filling-in' process has been proposed for brightness perception (Paradiso and Nakayama, 1991) and texture segregation (Lamme et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The Euclidean model holds that reaction time depends on the distance between cues, irrespective of the shape of the objects.
source: The fifth and final model is a Euclidean model, which will serve as reference because it is simple. It holds that the reaction time depends on the distance between cues, irrespective of the shape of the objects (Figure 2e).
evidence: This describes the Euclidean model as a reference model.

claim: In Experiment 1A, the average accuracy was 94%.
source: The average accuracy was 94%, without signs of a speed-accuracy trade-off (correlation between RT and accuracy; r=0.17, t(22)=0.80, p>0.4).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 1A, there were no signs of a speed-accuracy trade-off.
source: The average accuracy was 94%, without signs of a speed-accuracy trade-off (correlation between RT and accuracy; r=0.17, t(22)=0.80, p>0.4).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 1A, if the two cues fell on the 'same' wedge, RTs were shortest in the center of the wedge and longer near the edges.
source: If the two cues fell on the 'same' wedge, RTs were shortest in the center of the wedge and longer near the edges (repeated-measures ANOVA, Greenhuise-Geisser corrected, F(4.5, 85.7)=10.9, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: In Experiment 1A, RTs in the 'different' condition were longer than in the 'same' condition.
source: RTs in the 'different' condition were longer than in the 'same' condition (F(1,19)=19.5, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 1A, the growth-cone model accounted for 86% of the variance of the RTs.
source: A regression analysis revealed that the growth-cone model accounted for 86% of the variance of the RTs, which was significantly better than models predicting that RT is constant (p<0.001 bootstrap statistic, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis of the experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 1A, the growth-cone model was significantly better than models predicting that RT is constant.
source: A regression analysis revealed that the growth-cone model accounted for 86% of the variance of the RTs, which was significantly better than models predicting that RT is constant (p<0.001 bootstrap statistic, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by bootstrap statistical analysis.

claim: The Filling-in model predicted that RT is shortest near the edges, opposite to the RT data in Experiment 1A.
source: The Filling-in model predicted that RT is shortest near the edges, opposite to the RT data.
evidence: This compares model predictions to experimental data.

claim: In the control experiment for Experiment 1, edges did not act as a mask.
source: We did not observe a significant correlation between RT and the distance between cue and edge (r=−0.2, t(30)=−1.31, p>0.1). Thus, the edges did not act as a mask.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of control experiment data.

claim: In Experiment 1B, the average accuracy was 93%.
source: The average accuracy was 93% and we did not obtain evidence for a speed-accuracy trade off (correlation between RT and accuracy, r=0.02; t(62)=0.14, p>0.8).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 1B, there was no evidence for a speed-accuracy trade-off.
source: The average accuracy was 93% and we did not obtain evidence for a speed-accuracy trade off (correlation between RT and accuracy, r=0.02; t(62)=0.14, p>0.8).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 1B, the average RT was higher when the cue was farther from the fixation point.
source: The average RT was higher when the cue was farther from the fixation point and a further delay was observed near the edges (warm colors in Figure 4b), in line with the predictions of the growth-cone model (compare Figure 4b to the lower left panel of Figure 3c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: In Experiment 1B, a further delay was observed near the edges.
source: The average RT was higher when the cue was farther from the fixation point and a further delay was observed near the edges (warm colors in Figure 4b), in line with the predictions of the growth-cone model (compare Figure 4b to the lower left panel of Figure 3c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: In Experiment 1B, the filling-in model erroneously predicted that RTs are shortest near the edges.
source: The filling-in model erroneously predicted that RTs are shortest near the edges.
evidence: This compares model predictions to experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 1B, the Euclidean model accounted for 49% of the variance.
source: The Euclidean model (and the pixel-by-pixel model, which made the same prediction in this experiment) accounted for 49% of the variance but failed to explain the influence of edge vicinity.
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 1B, the Euclidean model failed to explain the influence of edge vicinity.
source: The Euclidean model (and the pixel-by-pixel model, which made the same prediction in this experiment) accounted for 49% of the variance but failed to explain the influence of edge vicinity.
evidence: This is an assessment of model performance based on experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 1B, the growth-cone model accounted for 72% of the variance.
source: The growth-cone model did capture this effect and it accounted for 72% of the variance.
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 4c.

claim: In Experiment 1B, the predictions of the growth-cone model were significantly better than those of the other models.
source: The predictions of the growth-cone model were significantly better than those of the other models (all ps<0.01 bootstrap statistic)
evidence: This is supported by bootstrap statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 1B, the average speed of perceptual grouping was 22 ms/growth cone (95% confidence interval 17–27 ms).
source: the regression revealed that the average speed of perceptual grouping was 22 ms/growth cone (95% confidence interval 17–27 ms, bootstrap analysis).
evidence: This is derived from regression analysis of experimental data.

claim: Grouping of surfaces invokes a serial perceptual grouping process that proceeds fast in homogeneous image regions and slows down near edges.
source: Thus, grouping of surfaces invokes a serial perceptual grouping process that proceeds fast in homogeneous image regions and slows down near edges, in accordance with the growth-cone model.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results of Experiment 1.

claim: Object recognition can provide larger chunks to be grouped at once.
source: Third, does object recognition affect perceptual grouping, because it can provide larger chunks to be grouped at once, as suggested by previous work (Mahoney and Ullman, 1988; Peterson and Gibson, 1994; Vecera and Farah, 1997; Korjoukov et al., 2012)?
evidence: This is a question based on prior research cited.

claim: In Experiment 2 with scrambled cartoons, the RT was shortest for the nearest cue (627 ms) and it increased by 24/30 ms for the more distant cues.
source: The RT was shortest for the nearest cue (blue in Figure 5b, 627 ms) and it increased by 24/30 ms (green/red in Figure 5b) for the more distant cues.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: In Experiment 2 with scrambled cartoons, the filling-in model made the wrong prediction that RT is shortest near boundaries (r=−0.30).
source: As in experiment 1, the filling-in model made the wrong prediction that RT is shortest near boundaries (r=−0.30).
evidence: This compares model predictions to experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 2 with scrambled cartoons, the Euclidean model showed a weak relationship (r=0.29).
source: The Euclidean model predicts that RT depends on the distance between fixation point and cue (i.e. the eccentricity of the cue) but this relationship was weak in the data (r=0.29).
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 2 with scrambled cartoons, the predictions of the pixel-by-pixel model were better (r=0.36) than the Euclidean model.
source: The predictions of the pixel-by-pixel model were better (r=0.36) but those of the growth-cone model were best (r=0.76).
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 5e.

claim: In Experiment 2 with scrambled cartoons, the growth-cone model was best (r=0.76).
source: The predictions of the pixel-by-pixel model were better (r=0.36) but those of the growth-cone model were best (r=0.76).
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 5f.

claim: In Experiment 2 with scrambled cartoons, the growth-cone model explained 58% of the variance.
source: The growth-cone model explained 58% of the variance, which was significantly better than the other three models (Figure 6a) (bootstrap statistic: all ps<0.01)
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 6a.

claim: In Experiment 2 with scrambled cartoons, the growth-cone model was significantly better than the other three models.
source: The growth-cone model explained 58% of the variance, which was significantly better than the other three models (Figure 6a) (bootstrap statistic: all ps<0.01)
evidence: This is supported by bootstrap statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 2 with scrambled cartoons, the estimated time per growth cone shift was 24 ms (95% confidence interval; 18–29 ms).
source: the regression yielded an estimated time per growth cone shift of 24 ms (95% confidence interval; 18–29 ms), in accordance with the estimate of Experiment 1.
evidence: This is derived from regression analysis of experimental data.

claim: Perceptual grouping of 2D image regions invokes a serial grouping process with a speed that depends on their scale.
source: Thus, perceptual grouping of 2D image regions invokes a serial grouping process with a speed that depends on their scale: wide regions are grouped quickly and narrow regions more slowly.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results of Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 2 with cartoon outlines, the growth cone model explained 41% of the variance.
source: We did, however, also test the cartoon images in 22 subjects (Figure 6b). The growth cone model explained 41% of the variance, which is more than any other model (bootstrap: all ps<0.01).
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 6b.

claim: In Experiment 2 with cartoon outlines, the growth cone model was better than any other model.
source: The growth cone model explained 41% of the variance, which is more than any other model (bootstrap: all ps<0.01).
evidence: This is supported by bootstrap statistical analysis.

claim: The growth cone model was not better than the other models for the detailed cartoons with interior contours and for the color pictures.
source: However, the growth cone model was not better than the other models for the detailed cartoons with interior contours and for the color pictures (Figure 6c,d).
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis shown in Figures 6c and 6d.

claim: The interior lines of the detailed cartoons and the colors and textures of the picture stimuli influence grouping speed.
source: These results reveal that the growth-cone model provides an excellent account for the pattern of RTs for scrambled cartoons and cartoon outlines, but that the predictions for the detailed cartoons (with internal contours) and colored pictures are worse. It follows that the interior lines of the detailed cartoons and the colors and textures of the picture stimuli influence grouping speed.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of model fits across different stimulus types.

claim: Grouping depends on the spread of object-based attention across the features that need to be bound in perception.
source: Previous studies suggested that grouping depends on the spread of object-based attention across the features that need to be bound in perception (Rensink, 2000; Roelfsema, 2006; Roelfsema et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Egly et al. (1994) found that if the cue was invalid and the target appeared at the other end of the cued bar, the response was faster than if it appeared at the non-cued bar.
source: Their main finding, however, was that if the cue was invalid and the target appeared at the other end of the cued bar (invalid same-object trials), the response was faster than if it appeared at the non-cued bar (invalid different-object trials), even if the distance between the target and the invalid cue was constant.
evidence: This describes a finding from prior research by Egly et al. (1994).

claim: The reaction-time difference between invalid same- and different object trials is a measure for object-based attention.
source: The reaction-time difference between invalid same- and different object trials is a measure for object-based attention, which is hypothesized to select the entire cued bar (Egly et al., 1994; Xu and Chun, 2007; Lamy and Egeth, 2002; Drummond & Shomstein 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies on object-based attention.

claim: In Experiment 3, the average accuracy across participants was 99%.
source: The average accuracy across participants was 99%.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 3, bar width did not influence RT on validly cued trials.
source: On validly cued trials, bar width did not influence RT (t(10)=−1.450, p>0.1; Figure 7b).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 7b.

claim: In Experiment 3, RTs were shorter on validly cued than invalidly cued trials.
source: As expected, RTs were shorter on validly cued than invalidly cued trials (t(10)=−3.468, p<0.01).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 3, RTs were shorter with invalid cues on the same object than on a different object.
source: We computed the object-based advantage for the broad and narrow bars and found that RTs were shorter with invalid cues on the same object than on a different object, an object-based advantage that is in accordance with previous studies (Egly et al., 1994; Xu and Chun, 2007; Lamy and Egeth, 2002; Drummond & Shomstein 2010).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and is consistent with prior research.

claim: In Experiment 3, the maximal object-based advantage occurred earlier for the broad bar than for the narrow bar.
source: The maximal object-based advantage occurred earlier for the broad bar than for the narrow bar (Figure 7c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7c.

claim: In Experiment 3, the object-based advantage peaked after 344 ms (95% confidence interval: 311–376 ms) for the broad bar.
source: We fitted a Gaussian function to the object-based benefit and found that it peaked after 344 ms (95% confidence interval: 311–376 ms) for the broad bar
evidence: This is derived from fitting analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 3, the object-based advantage peaked after 463 ms (434–492 ms) for the narrow bar.
source: and after 463 ms (434–492 ms) for the narrow bar (p<0.001; bootstrap analysis).
evidence: This is derived from fitting analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 3, the estimated speed of attention spreading was 31 ms per growth cone.
source: We estimated the speed of attention spreading by dividing the time difference of 119 ms by the difference in the estimated number of growth cones (7.2–3.3=3.9) and obtained a speed of 31 ms per growth cone, compatible with the speed estimates of Experiments 1 and 2.
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data.

claim: The new task revealed that perceptual grouping relies on a serial, incremental process, refuting the uniform connectedness rule proposed by Palmer and Rock, 1994.
source: The new task allowed us to measure the time course of grouping operations in simple 2D line drawings and revealed that perceptual grouping relies on a serial, incremental process, refuting the uniform connectedness rule proposed by Palmer and Rock, 1994.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Some forms of perceptual grouping related to the recognition of objects or image categories is very rapid and pre-attentive.
source: At first sight, such a slow, serial grouping process seems to be at odds with previous findings that some forms of perceptual grouping, related to the recognition of objects or image categories like animals and vehicles, is very rapid and pre-attentive (Thorpe et al., 1996; Kirchner and Thorpe, 2006; Moore and Egeth, 1997; Treisman, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Pre-attentive formation of perceptual groupings appears to rely on rapid feedforward computations that take place when visual information propagates from early to higher visual areas.
source: The pre-attentive formation of perceptual groupings appears to rely on rapid feedforward computations that take place when visual information propagates from early to higher visual areas (Yamins et al., 2014), a strategy that is also used by state-of-the-art convolutional networks for object recognition (Szegedy et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The recognition of objects in the scene does not imply that visual segmentation processes have completed.
source: However, the recognition of objects in the scene does not imply that visual segmentation processes have completed (Epshtein et al., 2008; Houtkamp and Roelfsema, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: It is difficult to compute connectedness in a purely feedforward manner.
source: For example, connectedness is one of the cues for perceptual grouping, and it is difficult to compute connectedness in a purely feedforward manner (Minsky and Papert, 1990; Roelfsema et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: If a scene contains multiple animals, the recognition of the species does not imply that all parts of every animal have been grouped as coherent percepts.
source: Furthermore, if a scene contains multiple animals, the recognition of the species does not imply that all parts of every animal have been grouped as coherent percepts (Korjoukov et al., 2012) because there are also cases where recognition precedes image parsing (Vecera and Farah, 1997; Peterson et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The visual system processes simple 2D image regions as miniature mazes.
source: Our results suggest that the visual system processes simple 2D image regions as miniature mazes, and for mazes serial processing is less surprising (Crowe et al., 2000).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results with a citation to related work.

claim: Serial processing has been observed in contour grouping tasks where grouping is associated with the gradual spread of object-based attention over the perceptual group.
source: Serial processing has also been observed previously in contour grouping tasks (Roelfsema, 2006), where grouping is associated with the gradual spread of object-based attention over the perceptual group (Figure 1a,b) (Houtkamp et al., 2003), a process that can only occur for one curve at a time (Houtkamp and Roelfsema, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In the visual cortex, the spread of attention is associated with the propagation of enhanced neuronal activity over the representation of the relevant curve.
source: In the visual cortex, the spread of attention is associated with the propagation of enhanced neuronal activity over the representation of the relevant curve (Pooresmaeili and Roelfsema, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to neurophysiological research.

claim: Spreading is fast if curves are far apart but it slows down if curves are in each other's vicinity.
source: Spreading is fast if curves are far apart but it slows down if curves are in each other's vicinity.
evidence: This is based on prior research on curve tracing.

claim: The curve-tracing operation has been modeled as a growth-cone process.
source: The curve-tracing operation has also been modeled as a growth-cone process, similar to the one we now used to model grouping of 2D image regions (Pooresmaeili and Roelfsema, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior modeling work.

claim: During object recognition, image parsing may be unnecessary, but during grasping one needs to determine whether surfaces belong to the same object.
source: In daily life, this serial grouping operation may only be necessary for specific tasks. During object recognition, image parsing may be unnecessary, but during grasping one needs to determine whether surfaces belong to the same object to avoid placing fingers on surfaces of different ones.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional role of serial grouping.

claim: The variation in the scale of processing could rely on multiple stages of the visual cortical hierarchy where neurons have different RF sizes.
source: The variation in the scale of processing could rely on multiple stages of the visual cortical hierarchy where neurons have different RF sizes (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: Near boundaries and in narrow parts of an object, the perceptual grouping process requires a high spatial resolution, which can be supported by small receptive fields in lower areas.
source: Near boundaries and in narrow parts of an object, the perceptual grouping process requires a high spatial resolution, which can be supported by small receptive fields in lower areas (purple and blue in Figure 8).
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal based on known properties of visual cortex.

claim: If the homogeneous image regions are larger, the propagation may take place in higher areas with larger RFs so that the grouping speed is higher.
source: If the homogeneous image regions are larger, the propagation may take place in higher areas with larger RFs so that the grouping speed is higher (red in Figure 8).
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal based on known properties of visual cortex.

claim: The scale dependence of the spread of object-based attention is in accordance with neuroimaging studies revealing the stronger engagement of lower visual areas when the relevant spatial scale is finer.
source: This scale dependence of the spread of object-based attention is in accordance with neuroimaging studies revealing the stronger engagement of lower visual areas when the relevant spatial scale is finer (Rijpkema et al., 2008; Hopf et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to neuroimaging studies.

claim: The growth-cone mechanism does not require the receptive field size to be constant within a visual cortical area.
source: Although the growth-cone model capitalizes on the presence of receptive fields with different sizes at distinct levels of the visual cortical processing hierarchy, it does not require the receptive field size to be constant within a visual cortical area.
evidence: This is a clarification about the model's assumptions.

claim: The size of receptive fields increases with eccentricity.
source: Indeed, it is well known that the size of receptive fields increases with eccentricity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about visual cortex organization.

claim: The horizontal distance between neurons with abutting, non-overlapping RFs is relatively constant across visual areas.
source: The horizontal distance between neurons with abutting, non-overlapping RFs is relatively constant across visual areas (Harvey and Dumoulin, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The propagation speed (in °/s or growth-cones/s) should be constant across eccentricities for a bar with a constant width.
source: Thus, if we assume that the propagation of enhanced neuronal activity through horizontal connections is also similar, it follows that the propagation speed (in °/s or growth-cones/s) should also be constant across eccentricities for a bar with a constant width.
evidence: This is an inference based on known properties of visual cortex.

claim: The growth-cone mechanism is compatible with the fact that the receptive field size in visual cortical areas increases with eccentricity.
source: The growth-cone mechanism is therefore compatible with the fact that the receptive field size in visual cortical areas increases with eccentricity.
evidence: This is an inference about the model's compatibility with known neuroscience.

claim: The current implementation of the growth-cone model is based on the outlines of the shapes only.
source: The current implementation of the growth-cone model is based on the outlines of the shapes only and, accordingly, the interior features of detailed cartoons and color pictures decreased fit quality.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the current model implementation.

claim: Interior contours might slow down parsing by presenting barriers or facilitate object recognition and thereby speed up the grouping.
source: The overall influence of the interior contours is difficult to predict, however. On the one hand, they might slow down parsing by presenting barriers. On the other hand, they might facilitate object recognition and thereby speed up the grouping.
evidence: This is speculation about possible effects of interior contours.

claim: Perceptual grouping with color pictures also relies on a serial process.
source: Importantly, perceptual grouping with the same color pictures also relies on a serial process (Korjoukov et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Models of segmentation can take advantage of recent breakthroughs in hierarchical convolutional neural networks for object recognition.
source: Models of segmentation can take advantage of the recent breakthroughs in hierarchical convolutional neural networks for object recognition (e.g. Krizhevsky et al. (2012); Zeiler and Fergus (2013); reviewed by LeCun et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent work in machine learning.

claim: Hierarchical convolutional networks consist of multiple hierarchically organized layers, which transform simple features at the lower layers to representations for shape recognition in higher layers.
source: These networks consist of multiple hierarchically organized layers, which transform simple features at the lower layers, resembling lower visual cortical areas, to representations for shape recognition in higher layers, resembling the inferotemporal cortex (Güçlü and van Gerven, 2015; Yamins and DiCarlo, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to research on neural networks and their relationship to visual cortex.

claim: Recent studies have started to apply hierarchical convolutional networks to achieve semantic segmentation.
source: Recent studies have started to apply hierarchical convolutional networks to achieve semantic segmentation (Hong et al., 2015; Noh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent work in computer vision.

claim: Semantic segmentation networks can segment pictures of everyday visual scenes.
source: The resulting networks can segment pictures of everyday visual scenes.
evidence: This is based on the capabilities of the cited networks.

claim: Semantic segmentation networks explain why object-recognition facilitates image parsing in human perception.
source: Hence, these models explain why object-recognition facilitates image parsing in human perception (Vecera and Farah, 1997; Peterson et al., 1991; Korjoukov et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference connecting computational models to human perception with citations.

claim: The deconvolutional network could be implemented in the visual cortex as a top-down influence from neurons in shape selective cortical areas to neurons in lower visual areas.
source: The deconvolutional network could be implemented in the visual cortex as a top-down influence from neurons in shape selective cortical areas to neurons in lower visual areas (i.e. generalizing the feedback connections in Figure 8) (Hochstein and Ahissar, 2002).
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal with a citation to prior work.

claim: Semantic segmentation networks may need to include horizontal connections to account for serial patterns of reaction times in grouping tasks with natural images.
source: We expect that semantic segmentation networks may need to also include horizontal connections in order to account for the serial patterns of reaction times in grouping tasks with natural images (as in Korjoukov et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculation about future model development with a citation.

claim: The parsing of a natural scene would invoke an incremental grouping process that gradually adds simple features and more complex shape fragments to an evolving perceptual group.
source: According to this view, the parsing of a natural scene would invoke an incremental grouping process that gradually adds simple features and more complex shape fragments to an evolving perceptual group (Roelfsema, 2006; Roelfsema and Houtkamp, 2011).
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal with citations to prior work.

claim: Experiment 3 confirmed that the spread of object-based attention depends on the size of image regions.
source: We conjectured that grouping relies on the spread of object-based attention within homogenous image regions, and this spread should therefore depend on the size of these regions. Our third experiment confirmed this prediction by showing that the spread of object-based attention is slower for narrow regions.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental results of Experiment 3.

claim: The spread of object-based attention is slower for narrow regions.
source: Our third experiment confirmed this prediction by showing that the spread of object-based attention is slower for narrow regions.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental results of Experiment 3.

claim: Experiment 3 yielded an estimate of the attentional propagation speed of ~30 ms per growth cone.
source: The last experiment yielded an estimate of the attentional propagation speed of ~30 ms per growth cone, which is similar to the estimates of 22 and 24 ms/growth cone of the other two experiments.
evidence: This is derived from the experimental data of Experiment 3.

claim: In V1, the distance between neurons with adjacent RFs is 2–4 mm.
source: In V1, the distance between neurons with adjacent RFs is 2–4 mm, and it is only slightly larger in higher visual areas (Hubel and Wiesel, 1974; Harvey and Dumoulin, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to neuroanatomical studies.

claim: The propagation speed is 8–16 cm/s (2–4 mm/ 25 ms).
source: Our results therefore suggest that the propagation speed is 8–16 cm/s (2–4 mm/ 25 ms), which falls neatly in the range of previous neurophysiological measures for the horizontal propagation of neuronal activity in visual cortex (Hirsch and Gilbert, 1991; Nauhaus et al., 2009; Sato and Carandini, 2012).
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data and compared to prior neurophysiological measurements.

claim: Perceptual grouping of 2D image regions calls on a serial process that takes tens to hundreds of milliseconds for naturalistic pictures.
source: Our results suggest that perceptual grouping of 2D image regions calls on a serial process that takes tens to hundreds of milliseconds for naturalistic pictures.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Subjects need time to spread object-based attention within the interior of image regions that need to be grouped in perception.
source: Subjects apparently need this time to spread object-based attention within in the interior of image regions that need to be grouped in perception.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results.

claim: The typical time between two saccadic eye movements is ~200–300 ms.
source: The typical time between two saccadic eye movements is ~200–300 ms
evidence: This is established knowledge about eye movement behavior.

claim: The duration of visual fixations may be optimized to allot time for both object recognition and image parsing before the next saccade is made.
source: and it is therefore tempting to speculate that the duration of visual fixations is optimized to allot time for both object recognition and image parsing before the next saccade is made.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of fixation durations.
